deep.reconstruction:
Context (from the previous and next pages): Gauss is evaluating a 'Decident', which is in effect a biquadratic character, by a lattice-point count in the Gaussian integers. On the previous page the multiples of p° are taken modulo a Gaussian integer of norm 8633 = 89·97. One can check that 52+77i = (8+5i)(9+4i), with 89 = 8²+5² and 97 = 9²+4². For each p° the 'Intensor' λ is recorded; it lies in {0,1,2,3} and acts as an exponent of i, i.e. which quarter the point falls in. The 'Theil des Decident' terms ±λ are then summed row by row, one row for each fixed Y°, giving 'Partialsummen'. The next page introduces the change of variables Dx = αX − 6Y, Dy = 6X + αY (the '6' is probably 𝔟 misread) and works examples.

Article 3. Fix an integer row Y° (take Y° even). In that row X runs from the boundary value X* to X**. The corresponding complex point p = x+iy runs continuously from p* to p**. The Gaussian integer part [p] changes only in jumps, each time x or y crosses an integer. Let these jump points be X* < X' < X'' < … < X^μ ≤ X**, with corresponding p', p'', …. Write λ* and λ** for the Intensors at the two ends. On the k-th segment the Intensor is constant:
- on (X*, X'] it is λ*;
- on (X', X''] it is λ*+δ';
- and so on, up to λ*+δ'+…+δ^μ = λ** on the last segment.

The margin notes settle the endpoint conventions:
- x increases along the segment, so an integer x** is counted at X^μ.
- y increases when 𝔟 > 0 (then y** is counted) and decreases when 𝔟 < 0 (then y* is counted).

The partial sum of the row is Σ (−1)^{X°} λ([p(X°)]) over the integers X° in the row. It therefore equals
 Σ_k λ_k (g_k − h_k),
where g_k and h_k count the even and odd integers X° in the k-th segment. Gauss writes this as λ*(g−h) + (λ*+δ')(g'−h') + … + λ**(g^μ−h^μ). For odd Y° the signs are reversed.

Article 4. Put f(t) = [t/2 − 1/2] − [t/2] (my notation). Then f(t) = −1 if [t] is even and f(t) = 0 if [t] is odd; this is the ε of the next page.

Step (mine): Σ_{n ≤ N} (−1)^n equals −1 for N odd and 0 for N even. Hence the number of even integers minus the number of odd integers in (a,b] is f(a) − f(b).

Substituting and regrouping by summation by parts (Abel summation), the partial sum becomes
 λ* f(X*) + δ' f(X') + δ'' f(X'') + … + δ^μ f(X^μ) − λ** f(X**).
This is exactly Gauss's display. Because the jumps now enter only through the products δ·f(X), the next page remarks that the jump points no longer need to be sorted.
errors: In the line for δ' the second bracket is written as a curly brace, {½X'}. This is a pen slip for the integer-part bracket [½X'], as in every other line.

g, h are defined only for the first segment, from X* to X'. The analogous g', h', … for the later segments, and the half-open convention (a,b] that makes Article 4 exact, are left implicit. Gauss handles the endpoints only through the marginal notes about counting x**, y** and y*.

The equality λ*+δ'+…+δ^μ = λ** appears to have a struck-through '='. The equality holds exactly only if λ is taken as a fixed representative in 0..3, so that δ ∈ {±1, ±3}. Otherwise it holds only mod 4. Either way the regrouped formula is unaffected, since it uses λ** directly.

results.what: The partial sum over a row of the sign-weighted Intensors is expressed through the jump points of the Gaussian integer part along the row.
results.modern_name: Piecewise-constant decomposition of a lattice-point sum (counting argument behind a Gauss-lemma-type evaluation of the biquadratic residue character)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss for the biquadratic lemma (Nachlass); lattice-point methods in reciprocity are associated with Gauss (third proof, 1808) and Eisenstein (1844).

results.what: The count of even minus odd integers in (a,b] equals f(a) − f(b), with f(t) = [t/2−1/2] − [t/2], and f(t) = −1 or 0 according as [t] is even or odd.
Regrouping Σ λ_k (f(X_k) − f(X_{k+1})) into λ* f(X*) + Σ δ_k f(X_k) − λ** f(X**).

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful, unpublished working-out of the lattice-point machinery for Gauss's own biquadratic Gauss-lemma approach. It is technically interesting, but it belongs to a research line known to be his from the Nachlass (Werke II/X and later studies). The individual steps (floor identities, summation by parts) are elementary.

transcription_corrections: In the second line of Article 4, read '[½X']' rather than '{½X'}'; the curly brace is a slip in the manuscript.
In the next-page formulas, 'Dx = αX − 6Y' and 'Dy = 6X + αY': the '6' is very probably 𝔟 (Fraktur b), the letter used on this page.
The fragment 'denen die Werthe von p' is a repetition: 'und denen' at the end of the line is resumed as 'denen die Werthe von p … entsprechen'.
The marginal 'falls' belongs to the struck-through line ('so wird die Partialsumme diese seyn'), not to the new text.
